scores.why: The sawn-apart cinder split across the two bookends is the one genuinely good idea here: a pair that is literally one object. But quarry cinder is a cheap, generic material and the piece reads as a nice paperweight until you know the story.

Yellow sulfur under an Acid lamina will photograph well, but a mineral specimen in a puck is the gift-shop embedment genre, and calling Sicilian sulfur 'Dallol' is a provenance fudge a serious collector will catch. Sulfur is also soft and reactive, which worries a conservator.
Conceptually coherent with the strata language, but a 2 mm sand bed is too quiet to sell itself on sight, and sand carries no scarcity. Better as a standard variant than an edition.
Burl wood in clear plastic is the epoxy river-table and Etsy cliche, and close to Nucleo's wood-in-a-block signature. It cheapens the house.

Pressed dried botanicals is the nearest thing in the set to flowers-in-acrylic, so it invites the Kuramata and Rusak comparison it cannot win, and the seed heads will brown and look tired in ten years.

scores.premium: +150-250% (meteorite cost plus story; roughly $2,500-4,000 over standard Core)
scores.why: An etched Widmanstatten slice floating at the centre of a ball called Core is the best story-to-object fit in the whole set, and the material has its own intrinsic, documented market value. Meteorite-in-lucite souvenirs exist, so the quality of the slice, the etch and the documented provenance must be impeccable; corrosion of the iron is the risk to engineer out.
A bought beach pebble in a puck has no scarcity and no surprise; it is a souvenir paperweight. Drop it.

Stacked lens voids after the frozen methane bubbles of Abraham Lake is an image people already love, rendered in a way only a laminator could do, and it owes nothing to Kuramata or Ariel. Value rests on the making being visibly difficult and flawless: each bubble clean, no cement creep, and a hand-drawn bubble map per number would make every piece unique.

An edge-lit gradient of fine voids will be beautiful in a room, but a glowing graded panel sits uncomfortably near Marcelis's luminous gradients and Wonmin Park's haze, and thousands of tiny voids is a process a competitor can copy. Good, not distinctive.

One silver pearl of air in a clear sphere is the most gallery-minded object here: silent, minimal, and arresting on a plinth. Its weakness is that it is a simple idea anyone could make, so its value depends on optical perfection (an invisible equator bond) and on EARF's name growing.

scores.edition_size: 8 per mountain (Shasta first, then a series)
scores.why: A real contour line drawn in air and lit from the edge is lovely and true to Relief, and the air-channel principle is free so long as the subject stays topographic, not Ariel-figurative. A series of named mountains, each a small edition, builds a collectible set.

scores.edition_size: 33 (for 33 1/3 rpm), each carrying a different consecutive slice of Session 00
scores.why: Sound made visible as a groove of air is exactly the rule's ideal: EARF's own world, arranged by EARF logic, impossible to mistake for anyone else. Make each number carry the next slice of the recording so the full edition, laid out, plays the first half-minute: that makes every piece unique and gives a reason to chase the set.

Strings of bubbles in a column is bullicante's grid turned vertical and reads as decorative rather than inevitable; 'rain on black lava' in Acid tint is a muddled image. A pleasant lamp, a weak edition.
Master tape is a real relic, but brown tape in Smoke is visually dull and its value depends entirely on Session 00 becoming famous, which it is not yet. Keep it for when the record has a reputation.

scores.edition_size: Fixed by the stamper: as many shards as one stamper yields, about 12-16, numbered by position
scores.premium: +150% (and a stamper map showing where each shard came from)
scores.why: A mirror shard that physically pressed the record catches light with diffraction colour, is finite by nature, and a buyer understands its scarcity instantly. Framed stampers exist as music memorabilia, so the setting in a clear stand at eye level and the map of the cut stamper are what lift it to a design object.

A unique relic with a good story, but a stylus is nearly invisible, so the object has to be explained before it is wanted. Sell it once, to the right person, as part of a Session 00 set, not as an edition.

The factory's own rock record is honest, beautiful in colour, and costs almost nothing in materials, which makes the genesis story do all the work. It has real value only as a first-and-never-again edition tied to the founding run.
A printed drawing sealed in acrylic is the deal-toy tombstone the prior-art note warns against. It reads as corporate commemoration, not as an object.

notes: The strongest editions are the ones only a laminator could make (designed air) and the ones whose contents are finite relics of EARF's own first record; specimens bought from dealers or beaches read as paperweights and should mostly be cut. Launch small and coherent: B1, B5 and C2 together as a 'Session 00' trio on Moho and Bedrock, with A6 as the single high-ticket piece, rather than all seventeen at once, which would look like a catalogue, not a statement. Make every number in an edition different (consecutive waveform slices, bubble maps, shard positions) so collectors chase sets and the secondary market has something to talk about. Perfection of the bonds is the whole value proposition: one hazy bond line or cement-filled void and the piece is a craft fair object, so set a rejection standard and destroy failures publicly. Drop A4, A5, A7 and C5 outright; they invite comparisons to Nucleo, Rusak and the deal toy that EARF cannot win.
